deckinfo.name: Evil or Not (Tempo Control)
deckinfo.primer:
Dech tech: https://youtu.be/Yzz3mn8ro8w?si=payLu6dftGFlV2XE


Deck objective: Control the board via minions + removal magic + powerful "hate" sites


Win condition: Attack with [[Persecutor]] + occasional minion or magic damage


Will be updating Matchups as I get more experience with certain Avatars:


"Favorable" Matchups

Non-water decks - [[Earthquake]] and [[Cave-In]] are online

[[Avatar of Air]] - You can remove all of their minions before they get use out of them

[[Necromancer]] - [[Skeleton]]s and other Evil minions give you free movement all game

[[Geomancer]] - Can remove all minions and stand on top of them when they want to [[Craterize]]

[[Bladedancer]] - Can bury their equipment; You will most likely be on their side of the board and that will not allow them to get the second attack most of the time


"Even" Matchups

[[Sorcerer]] - Steam specifically is tough because of the damage and Ward minions; usually able to 2 or 3 for 1 enough times to mitigate their card advantage; [[Garden of Eden]]

[[Pathfinder]] - Mono-fire list can sometimes be too fast and too consistent


"Hard' Matchups

[[Battlemage]] - 3 power unkillable Avatar can lead to some dead draws if you only have removal

[[Archimago]] - Need [[Kor Crematory]] or [[Garden of Eden]] to stand a chance

[[Sparkmage]] - Can deal damage to your Avatar much faster than you can deal to them because of their tap ability


Artifacts

[[Crucifix]]: Able to bounce Evil minions (or minions you brand as Evil); [[Lord of Lies]] can't be summoned on top of you; can also brand an enemy Evil so they can't move and defend against an attack

[[Devil's Egg]]: Speeds up the game

[[Peacemaker Arbalest]]: Excellent for killing minions or doing damage to the enemy Avatar (ranged helps preserve life points)

[[Love Potion]]: "Poor man's [[Mesmerism]]"; [[Persecutor]] step ability allows you to freely move into a site and steal something strong


Minions

[[Arjaro Exorcist]]: Ability to banish Auras and Spirits is huge since Spirits aren't Evil; also helps cast magics

[[Kettletop Leprechaun]]: One of the best Earth minions in the game; allows you to draw spells and not sites

[[Vile Imp]]: Death's Door finisher; Evil minion to help [[Persecutor]] take a step; helps against aggressive decks

[[Colicky Dragonettes]]: Death's Door finisher; able to ping minions/tokens or the enemy Avatar

[[Morgana le Fay]]: Good card but not super necessary in the deck since we usually only cast 1 card a turn (sometimes 2)

[[Quarrelsome Kobolds]]: Death's Door finisher; able to help against aggressive decks; can do 4 damage on turn 4 if not removed

[[Root Spider]]: Disable good; helps move [[Devil's Egg]] under opponent's site

[[Hillock Basilisk]]: Ward remover; able to control the site it is on and the one in front of it; can attack the minion it is disabling

[[Hotwheel]]: Death's Door finisher; Evil minion

[[Asmodeus]]: Able to deal with any minions that are in my backline; Evil minion

[[Balor of the Evil Eye]]: Death's Door finisher; Evil minion; Damage is relevant to remove tokens or Wards

[[Infernal Legion]]: Death's Door finisher; Evil minion; Can potentially clear stealth minions


Magics

[[Immolation]]: 1 mana removal

[[Firebolts]]: Removal or damage to race

[[Begone!]]: Best removal in the game

[[Deliverance]]: Can be one sided board wipe; [[Persecutor]] can brand an enemy minion as Evil so it can be banished

[[Disintegrate]]: More removal

[[Cave-In]]: For grouped up minion on land sites; Can bury Devil's Egg so it is harder to get rid of

[[Firebreathing]]: Can damage minions and the enemy Avatar at the same time; can be cast by [[Hillock Basilisk]], [[Root Spider]], and [[Colicky Dragonettes]]

[[Earthquake]]: Potential board wipe; Site manipulation

[[Lava Flow]]: Devastating amount of damage to the enemy Avatar and can remove minions on the surface and subsurface

[[Poison Nova]]: Often times a board wipe given [[Persecutor]]'s mobility

[[Powerwish]]: Fun card that can clear the board of all minions even if Warded


Sites

Deserts: 1 damage for Wards or for damage math

[[Boulevard of Bones]]: Creates [[Skeleton]]s so [[Persecutor]] can take a step

[[Bureau of Occult Control]]: Hate site to slow down [[Imposter]], [[Archimago]], etc. and anyone using Collection access cards

[[City of Traitors]]: Helps get you to 5 mana faster; can put a [[Root Spider]] under

[[Fields of Camlann]]: Brings enemy minions down to 1 usually so my [[Begone]] or [[Disintegrate]] clears the board

[[Forge]]: Good on turn 1; can help with some attacks

[[Funeral Pyre]]: More cemetery hate

[[Garden of Eden]]: Helps against [[Battlemage]], [[Archimago]], and [[Sorcerer]]

[[Glastonbury Tor]]: Threshold

[[Kor Crematory]]: Shuts off [[Archimago]] and [[Deathspeaker]]

[[Molten Maar]]: 1 of for the occasional movement or when I don't have anything else to do on turn 3

[[Open Grave]]: [[Skeleton]] for movement

[[Pillar of Zeiros]]: More cemetery hate and potential healing

[[River of Blood]]: Gaining life is cheating

[[Steppe]]: Threshold


Collection

[[Carrion Beetles]]: Cemetery hate

[[Dispel]]: Gets rid of problem artifacts and auras

[[Vandal Imp]]: Good when there is only 1 artifact on the board; Evil minion

[[Boil]]: Removal against water decks

[[Bury]]: Removal against minions on landsites or to bury artifacts

[[Flame Strike]]: Death's Door finisher; hits [[Imposter]] when they put on [[Pathfinder]] mask

[[Hellhounds]]: For the 1 of [[Molten Maar]]

[[Minor Explosion]]: Death's Door finisher

[[Angry Mob]]: Removes problem Elite and Unique minions

[[Smite]]: Can do damage or banish in conjunction with [[Persecutor]] branding ability

deckinfo.name: Drown in the Deep
deckinfo.primer:
6/4/2026 -The Road to Gen Con


The meta continues to shift, and as it does, so too does this list! New tech has risen from the deep thanks to other Waveshapers piloting various lists, and its time Drown adapted. More notes at the end!


Drown in the Deep

Because Fun is Only For You


Drown in the Deep is a hard control deck focused on stalling out the early game through the repeated submerge effect of [[Mariner's Curse]] and [[Thin Ice]] alongside multiple forced movement effects to prevent your opponent's units from gaining a foothold in your territory. Once we've achieved complete control of the board, we shift our game plan to deploying our late-game threats and ending the game in one or two massive attacks.


This is a deck for people who enjoy controlling the chess match of Sorcery, using positioning and clever movement to send their opponent's forces below the waves, all while overwhelming them with the inevitability of enormous threats like [[Diluvian Kraken]] and [[Great Old One]].


A Note Before We Begin...


The current list of this deck is built with the assumption you will be taking it into a blind meta where you expect to see other meta decks. Currently, it is in testing for the post-Gothic summer meta, where mono-water Necromancer has come down some in the meta and Interrogator and Earth Ramp lists have risen in power.


This meta is still fairly favorable to our strategy than the previous. The primary concessions to the meta that the list makes are:

  • 2 copies of [[Mismanaged Mortuary]] in the Atlas - these cards only exist to hate out cemetery decks like Archimago
  • 2 copies of [[Return to Nature]] in the mainboard and 1 in the collection - while these spells can be useful when paired with [[Deep-Sea Mermaids]], they are primarily here to hate on Archimago
  • 1 copy of [[Makeshift Barricade]] in the collection - with the prevalence of [[Zap!]] as a Death's Door finisher, it's important we have a way to live if they drop us to zero. Makeshift barricade is that way.


Deck Philosophy


Drown in the Deep is structured in pillars. These pillars represent the core elements of the deck's game plan, and cards must fit into at least one aspect of these pillars to be considered for the list. The pillars of the deck's strategy are:


  1. Card Advantage: a nebulous concept in Sorcery. With card draw effects limited in scope, or paired with significant downsides, it's difficult to find consistent draw engines. As a result, we operate on pseudo-card advantage. Our goal is to turn each of our cards into X for 1's - meaning each card we play trades for more than 1 card our opponent plays. In this way, we will slowly rip away their resources without significantly reducing ours.
  2. Board Control: in Sorcery, we need to fight on two axes: removal and positioning. With our removal centralized in submerge effects, we rely on robust forced-movement tools to trigger our removal effects like Mariner's Curses, or cluster enemies for mass removal spells like [[Stormy Seas]] and [[Call of the Sea]].
  3. Threats: as a control deck, Drown has very few threats compared to mid-range or aggro decks. Most of our units are role players, existing within one of the other axes. Therefore, we rely on the following primary threats to end the game: [[Anui Undine]], [[Lord of Lies]], [[Mester Stoor Worm]], [[Vatn Draconis]], [[Diluvian Kraken]], and [[Great Old One]]. Protecting these units should be top of mind when they hit table, as they are our route to victory.
  4. Death's Door Solutions: without access to the direct damage many other elements provide in Sorcery, mono-water can sometimes struggle to kill our opponents while on Death's Door. As a result, this pillar is incredibly small, but incredibly important. Our primary Death's Door solutions lie in the activated abilities of units like [[Mester Stoor Worm]] and [[Diluvian Kraken]], but we keep additional methods of ending the game in our collection, to be played at the perfect moment by a [[Silver Bullet]] or [[Toolbox]]. These solutions will be discussed in the section on the Collection.


Strategy


With these pillars in mind, the deck's game plan simplifies into a three-phase process:


  1. Gain Control
  2. Maintain Control
  3. Kill Them


Navigating this process is anything but simple, however, so let's break down each step.


Gain Control


Gaining control relies on establishing two key pieces: a source of card advantage and a source of removal. In an ideal scenario, we'll draw the card that is both of these pieces in one: [[Mariner's Curse]].


Every time the Curse drowns a unit, it represents a card gained. Because it always returns to our hand, we can redeploy it every turn, constantly draining our opponent's draws by running them out of their valuable units. However, Mariner's Curse gets significantly worse if we're only drowning one thing a turn, which is where our forced movement effects come into play.


Pairing the Curse with [[Coy Nixie]], [[Guile Sirens]], [[Abaddon Succubus]], [[River Rapids]], [[Innsmouth Dock]] or [[Maelström]] presents repeatable removal on our turns, allowing us to use our mana to redeploy the Curse to protect our sites on their turns. Keep in mind that they will likely throw away their least valuable unit on their turn, so we need to identify their most valuable unit each turn and plan for ways to submerge them on our turn.


For a card so critical to our strategy, you may be wondering why we only run two copies in our Spellbook. Simply put, it's because the card is so valuable, we actually want to run four copies of Mariner's Curse. As a result, [[Silver Bullet]] represents copies three and four of Mariner's Curse, and will almost always be used to grab the copy that sits in our collection if we have not drawn one of the two copies in our Spellbook.


When the Curse isn't available, we need to identify ways to survive without it. [[Thin Ice]] is the strongest of our alternate Mariner's Curses, as Coy Nixie can drag any minion our opponent plays with three or more power directly to the Thin Ice and drown them at end of turn. In a pinch, [[Troll Bridge]] can do a decent impression, especially if we can deploy forced movement effects to trigger it on our turn. Clustering units together with our forced movement effects can turn [[Stormy Seas]] into a multi-card removal spell, while [[Nelly Longarms]] can act like [[Pudge Butcher]] and deal with any problematic units.


Additionally, an old card has found new power in the modern meta: [[Giant Shark]]. While this card can prevent us from developing our own units, deploying it on turn 5 can often bring the game to a complete standstill. The opponent will likely need to throw at least 2 cards into our shark just to clear it, and that means the Shark often does a fantastic impression of Mariner's Curse. Combined with forced movement, we can send the shark where we want it, when we want it.


Maintain Control


Once initial control is established, we need to begin identifying the ways our opponent can take that control away from us, and focus on preventing such circumstances from occurring. The primary goals of this phase of the game are to reach six mana and to avoid Death's Door.


Avoiding Death's Door is obvious: while our deck has dozens of tools to stave off units, we have zero tools to prevent direct spell damage. If our opponent is relying on units to kill us, we can stall out the game for a long time on Death's Door, but if they have anything to directly hit us, the game ends immediately. Preventing this scenario is one of our top priorities. [[Font of Life]] can be critical in this stage, usually representing a swing of seven or more life. It's also critical to identify which units you're comfortable losing, and being prepared to sacrifice them to avoid taking damage from strikes. [[Plague of Frogs]] is an all-star here, representing up to seven prevented attacks if the opponent can't find a way to remove our annoying little frogs.


Getting to six mana is a less obvious goal, but quickly becomes apparent as you draw through the deck: much of our curve exists at three mana. Reaching six mana means we can cast two spells a turn, and more importantly it means we can both deploy a unit and redeploy Mariner's Curse. As a result, this phase of the game is a constant dance between taking turns to deploy additional sites in preparation and using our Avatar to prevent multiple units from untapping. [[Riptide]] is great here; you can draw a spell for turn, play Riptide to cluster several units onto the same site, and draw a site off Riptide's effect to deploy the following turn. [[Overflow]] also shines in this phase. Each copy we play represents a turn where we can use our Avatar to tap down our enemies without risk of slowing down our curve progression.


This phase is also where we are looking for means to shut our opponent out of the game, or dig for our important threats. [[Atlantean Fate]] can shut down our opponent's game plan, stifling their threshold and drowning key units and artifacts. [[Mester Stoor Worm]] can use its tap ability to wipe out our opponent's armies every turn, while also holding onto a threat when we reach phase three. [[Stormy Seas]] can not only deal with problematic units, but take away important artifacts from our opponent by sending them below the water, where they are unlikely to have a means to retrieve them. Finally, [[Call of the Sea]] and [[Wrath of the Sea]] represent massive board wipes that can reset the board the turn before we're ready to bring down our biggest threats.


To help us dig for these key cards, we can leverage our Rivers to filter through our deck, [[Deep-Sea Mermaids]] to draw cards we mulliganed away early, and [[Kelp Cavern]] to setup a critical draw of an end-game threat when it's time to enter our final phase. Don't overlook the power of [[Return to Nature]] in this phase either. We can use it to put key cards we've already played back on the bottom of the deck, only to gain immediate access to them through our Deep-Sea Mermaids.


Kill Them


With control established and maintained, we can finally take turns off from controlling the board to develop our end-game threats. Of our end-game threats, the best combination we can hope to see is [[Vatn Draconis]] and [[Diluvian Kraken]].


Both of these threats represent units that exist in multiple pillars - Board Control and Threats. Vatn Draconis can submerge everything at its location, often killing multiple units the turn he enters play if we've clustered them correctly. Diluvian Kraken can surface every other turn to wipe out a 3x3 grid of units, while also damaging our opponent's avatar if we've positioned it correctly.


However, when paired together, these units get much more potent. We can surface the Kraken to strike all units nearby, and then surface Vatn Draconis to attack the surface of an opponent's site. Then, at end of turn, we can submerge everything at Vatn Draconis's site, including our own Kraken, allowing us to do it again.


Vatn Draconis is also important because it protects our units from removal effects like [[Disintegrate]], [[Poison Nova]], and [[Infiltrate]]. Unless our opponent has a submerged spell caster, they can't target or affect any of our submerged units.


Once we've dropped them to Death's Door, we deploy any of our methods to deal the final blow to their Avatar: [[Mester Stoor Worm]], [[Diluvian Kraken]]'s tap ability, or [[Toolbox]]. Make sure you're careful with how you deploy these effects before you're ready to kill your opponent - the last thing you want is to be staring down defeat because you prematurely used the only tool you had to end the game.


The Collection


The Collection mechanic is the single biggest improvement Drown in the Deep received from Gothic. The ability to guarantee specific cards, or draw out certain answers when we need them, has fundamentally altered this deck's power level. The two main ways we access the collection are [[Silver Bullet]] and [[Toolbox]], and we diversify the options we have in our Collection to ensure both present useful options whenever we draw them.


Drown's collection can be grouped into three categories: Extra Copies, Key Answers, and Death's Door Solutions.


Extra Copies


[[Mariner's Curse]], [[Swap]], and [[Stormy Seas]] are so good for our strategy that we want to see more than the normal number of copies we're allowed to run. As a result, they both take a Collection slot so that Silver Bullet can represent additional copies of them if we have yet to see our main deck copies.


[[Overflow]] also fits in this category, though not for the same reasons as the previous cards. While Overflow is excellent, it is strongest in the earliest turns of the game, and can be a dead draw later in the game. As a result, running only three in the spellbook reduces the likelihood we draw additional copies when we don't want them, but running one in the collection lets us turn an early [[Toolbox]] into well-timed ramp.


Key Answers


Historically, Drown struggled against two things: Site Destruction and Submerge units. Not every deck runs these mechanics, so finding slots for answers to them was always difficult. Thanks to the collection, we can shove these cards out of the main deck so we only draw them when we need them.


[[Sleep]] can help us disable a submerge unit so we can immediately drown them, while also letting us answer problematic minions like an [[Old Salt Anchorman]]. [[Swap]] can let us deal with an artifact or unit that is out of our reach, while also presenting lethal if we have a unit that can attack their avatar by removing a single blocker.


While strong in the mainboard, [[Return to Nature]] isn't quite strong enough that we want to draw multiple copies in a single game. However, against specific decks (like Archimago), drawing Return to Nature is absolutely critical. As a result, we can dedicate one slot in the collection to it so that Toolbox can help us find it in these specific scenarios, similar to our approach to Overflow.


Death's Door Solutions


We rarely, if ever, want to draw ways to kill our opponent when they aren't already on Death's Door. Cards like [[Ice Lance]] and [[Meat Hook]] are terrible cards if we draw them at the wrong time, but can end games out of nowhere if we draw them exactly when we need them. As a result, they exist in the Collection to help us kill our opponent at exactly the right moment.


Mulligans


In the early game, we need to find any source of card advantage we can muster. We almost always mulligan away big threats, with the intent of pulling them from the bottom of the deck at key points with Deep-Sea Mermaids or [[Kelp Cavern]]. For sites, Thin Ice, Troll Bridge, and [[Maelström]] are hyper critical to this deck, so we want to dig hard for them.


Why Waveshaper?


You may be wondering why [[Waveshaper]] is the avatar of choice for this deck. Ultimately, she does double duty. Her first role is to extend our body of water when we don't have a flooding effect handy. Her second role is to lock down units, buying us turns as our opponent's threats are prevented from tapping out. Once we reach our critical threshold of mana, Waveshaper can lock down our opponent's ground forces, potentially indefinitely if we have placed our forced movement effects correctly.


However, there are opportunities to replace Waveshaper with another Avatar, especially depending on your meta. If you're up against a lot of spell-based aggro or control decks, you may find better success with the additional movement opportunities of [[Avatar of Water]]. If your meta runs a lot of water decks, you may not need the flooding to extend your body of water, and might find more success with [[Sorcerer]] or [[Seer]] to fix card advantage. Finally, if you're up against a lot of decks with [[Summoning Sphere]] effects, you may consider [[Dragonlord]] with [[Vatn Draconis]] as your iconic dragon, which allows your avatar to spend 3 mana to drown everything on your site.


Matchup Advice


Pending further testing! All the matchups I used to give advice on are irrelevant now. I'll update this section when I've got sufficient reps against decks I expect you will see at big events.


Making the List Your Own

Note: this section is slightly outdated. The general advice still applies, but the specific assumptions and trends haven't been updated for the most recent version of the list. I'll update it when the list lands again in a concrete place!


In a shocking turn of events, I'm not the only one who wants to play Control Waveshaper anymore! With the deck as strongly positioned as it is, and the unique play style it offers, more people have begun picking up the list to pilot. As such, I wanted to include a brief section on how to change this list to suit your local meta.


First, I want to clarify something important: there are very few cards in this list that are "must" includes. The beauty of mono water Waveshaper post-Gothic is that it has a plethora of threats and options available to it, something that couldn't be said in previous metas. While there are certainly cards that are better suited to the moment, this is changing constantly, and the exact cards in this version of the list are shaped by what I believe the meta will present to me. As an example, more than 50% of this list changed post-Gothic because the meta shifted away from pure hyperaggro and towards grindier, midrange strategies. That allowed me to remove the less consistent, but sometimes more powerful, explosive ramp like Mixes and Four Waters and focus on the slower, inevitable build-up to eight mana.


That then, is where I begin this section: by examining the assumptions and trends that led this list to this exact set of cards. At the time of writing, my testing and the overall trends in the Gothic meta have led me to identify the following core challenges the deck has to prepare to face:


  1. The primary decks doing well in the meta are midrange, grindy decks like Necromonsters.
  2. Water is abundant in the meta, but few people are running Submerge threats, relying instead on generic good stuff cards to carry their games.
  3. The meta is still fast enough that we can't rely on efficient removal and blocking to stay off Death's Door alone; life gain still matters against many decks
  4. The deck's worst matchups, Mono-Fire Aggro and Archimago, are still present in the meta.
  5. Decks that rely on Auras like Enchantress are fringe enough that we don't need to worry much about them.


It goes without saying that if the above assumptions are not true about your local meta, you likely need to adjust this list accordingly, and plan to bring out different threats, answers, or even early game strategies. A control deck's gameplan is always dictated by the meta in which it exists, and Drown in the Deep is no different.


Those assumptions lead me to the following four conclusions, each corresponding to the assumptions I listed above.


  1. Necromonsters is exactly the kind of deck we want to see across the table from us. Their gameplan of developing a few key threats and protecting them is exactly the kind of deck we are tailored to beat. With even mediocre draws, playing Drown against a Necromonsters player usually feels like a game where we can't lose. We certainly still can - see my day 2 round against CJ on Necromonsters as an example - but the odds are stacked in our favor.
  2. With Water so abundant, but Submerge so rare, most players are counting on cards like [[Drown]] and [[Stormy Seas]] to kill problematic units. Therefore, we can blank a significant portion of our opponent's draws simply by relying on Submerge threats. However, Submerge threats aren't so rare that we can ignore the possibility we will sit down across from them. We need to have answers available that deal with Submerge units, in case other fringe decks in the meta come to the same conclusion we do.
  3. [[Font of Life]] and similar stall tactics are still a must play. With the prevalence of [[Zap]] in collections, and the switch to a 60-card spellbook, we can't rely on pre-Gothic strategies like [[Amulet of Niniane]] and [[Blasted Oak]] to stay alive on Death's Door. The only route to victory is to stay off Death's Door as long as possible.
  4. While our game plan against both of our worst matchups improved significantly through the plethora of new forced movement and card advantage engines Gothic provided, we still struggle into both Mono-Fire Aggro and Archimago. Sometimes, Mono-Fire Aggro builds a strong enough board fast enough that we never get to stabilize, and Archimago has a faster, more consistent endgame plan for victory than we do. This means we can't afford to sacrifice our methods of clawing back life and advantage, but we also can't give up our graveyard hate, especially [[Mismanaged Mortuary]]
  5. If Enchantress was dominating the meta, we would need to splash Air to make room for [[Disenchant]]. However, Auras remain a fringe strategy, and we can answer most artifacts simply by submerging them, so we maintain the mono-water plan, accepting that we may have some games where we have to fight from behind if the opponent plays a card like [[Drought]].


I provide this context for the simple answer to the question of how to make the deck your own: begin by identifying the trends that define your local meta, or the meta of a major tournament you plan to attend. From there, you can establish the things your deck needs to exist in that meta, and the tools required to dominate it. Once you have an idea of what tools you need to bring, you get to the true answer of any deck-building process: lots and lots of testing.


I hope this insight helps you customize the deck to be your own. The last thing I'll include in this section is a breakdown of how I rate each card in the deck, grouping them into the categories of Core Strategy, Best-in-Slot, and Flex Spots.


Core Strategy - The Cards That Define the Feel of the Deck

  1. Forced Movement - [[Coy Nixie]], [[Guile Sirens]], [[Nelly Longarms]], [[Abaddon Succubus]], [[Riptide]], [[Call of the Sea]], [[Innsmouth Dock]], [[Maelström]], [[River Rapids]], [[Undertow]]
  2. Card Advantage - [[Mariner's Curse]], [[Algor Omphalos]], [[Dank Omphalos]], [[Deep-Sea Mermaids]], [[Maiden, Mother, Crone]], [[Kelp Cavern]], [[Thin Ice]], [[Troll Bridge]], [[Watery Grave]], [[Autumn River]], [[Spring River]], [[Summer River]]
  3. Removal - [[Mariner's Curse]], [[Atlantean Fate]], [[Stormy Seas]], [[Call of the Sea]]
  4. Threats - [[Anui Undine]], [[Mester Stoor Worm]], [[Vatn Draconis]], [[Diluvian Kraken]], [[Great Old One]]


Best In Slot - Cards That Aren’t Directly Synergistic and Don’t Define the Feel, but Are Incredible in the Meta

  1. [[Ring of Morrigan]] - Broken beyond belief. Life gain, removal, Death's Door Solutions, this ring does it all. Combine it with the fact we can cast a single Mariner's Curse multiple times in a turn later in the game, and it gets even better.
  2. [[Silver Bullet]] and [[Toolbox]] - these cards let us move answers we normally don't get to run out of the main deck where they would be abysmal draws, and let us draw some of our best cards more often.
  3. [[Hyperparasite]] - one of the strongest ways to deal with enemy Submerge units, while also offering efficient, repeated removal of anything our opponent plays. Attacking disabled units is strong, and Hyperparasite does that all day!
  4. [[Lilith]] - sometimes, the best card you can play is your opponent's top card. The likelihood that you spend 5 mana to develop 2 bodies and go up a card is incredibly high. At her worst, she filters away spells our opponent might have wanted to see, increasing the likelihood they draw minions, which we're better equipped to handle anyways.
  5. [[Lord of Lies]] - a broken ability stapled to a six power body is a threat we love to see. He might not have submerge, but combined with our forced movement effects, we can easily move him into position to kill key threats our opponent plays. Plus, he can kill them while they're on Death's Door.
  6. [[The Green Knight]] - what if your forced movement effects ALSO fought the things they moved? That's the Green Knight for you! Drop it in a problematic spot and watch as their armies run themselves through on his sword.
  7. [[Plague of Frogs]] - seven blockers is dumb. This card frequently gains me 30-40 life just by eating a ton of attacks that would have gone at my face.
  8. [[Return to Nature]] - while this card is great for helping us survive the Archi matchup, it also lets us put key cards on the bottom of our library to draw back out with Deep-Sea Mermaids.
  9. [[Font of Life]] - this card literally gains us 30-40 life. The first Font of Life is usually a 3 mana spell that reads "target opponent skips their previous turn." The second usually reads "target opponent concedes because you're an awful person."
  10. [[Overflow]] - Ramp is important in a deck that needs to hit eight mana, and ramping while also letting us draw a site, reducing the number of turns we have to spend our draw step on picking up a site, is awesome.
  11. [[Swap]] - DD solution, Artifact Removal, and more all rolled into one. Great card, and I'd run three if I could ever figure out what to cut.
  12. [[Mesmerism]] - Secretly an extra way to kill Submerge threats, this can also be a rapid turnaround of life by stealing one of their units and turning it into a blocker for us.
  13. [[Wrath of the Sea]] - when the meta turns grindy and midrange, board wipes shine, and there is no better board wipe than Wrath of the Sea. With our plethora of ways to extend our body of water, this usually sends every minion and every artifact to the bottom of the sea.
  14. [[Babbling Brook]] - Disabling units means this site usually blanks our opponent's entire turn. The more turns they skip, the more turns we have to take control of the game.
  15. [[Island Leviathan]] - An eight power monster that only becomes vulnerable when we're ready to kill our opponent is a great way to turn [[Abyssal Assault]] into a guaranteed kill.
  16. [[Mirror Realm]] - we have so many broken sites that being able to play an extra copy of our best one is always welcome.
  17. [[Mismanaged Mortuary]] - the card that singlehandedly saves our Archimago matchup. By the time they answer this, we're usually ready to kill them anyways.


Flex Spots - Cards That Testing Has Shown Are the Best at Their Cost and Role, but Might Not Be the Best for Your Meta

  1. [[Lacuna Entity]] - It might only eat things 3 power and less, but a lot of cards we hate run around at 3 power or less. Drowning an Aggro Player's Charge threat, or Banishing an enemy Coy Nixie, or anything in between lets the Entity trade for a card immediately and serve as a block the next turn.


Change Log and Current Testing


2.4 - Road to Gen Con


As the meta continues to shift, and other Waveshapers find innovations I hadn't considered, it's time for the list to adapt once again. I'm going to break these changes into cuts and additions this time, as the swapped cards aren't quite as one-to-one this time around.


Cuts:

-2 [[Lacuna Entity]]

  • With the rise of ramp decks and the continued prevalence of midrange, it is rare that Lacuna Entity gets any value at all, and often represents a worse draw than almost any other minion in the deck.

-1 [[Anui Undine]]

  • While still an absolute Power House of a unit, the list doesn't often want to draw a unit that reads "beat up target player" in the mid game. Reducing her count reduces the likelihood we draw her before we're ready to enter the end game.

-2 [[Font of Life]]

  • Turns out, the meta still isn't fast enough to require drawing a card that is blank the vast majority of the games. We are long past the days of Steam Druid, and that means Font of Life returns to being a collection only card

-1 [[Order of the Sacred Oak]] (collection)

  • While a strong card, I have never cast this unit in any game I've played, and I've played a lot of games since the collection was added. Removed to make room for more relevant answers.

-1 [[Snowball]] (collection)

  • I've never had a game where I wanted to use Silver Bullet purely to kill my opponent. Cutting Snowball as a result.

-1 [[Grievous Insult]] (collection)

  • This is still a great card, and in a different meta, would likely have its place in the collection over [[Swap]] number three. As it stands, I think Swap is better positioned, so Grievous gets the axe.

-1 mainboard [[Swap]]

  • While a powerful card, we don't always want to see this as a top deck, and there are powerful cards we'd rather see from our deck. One Swap is cut from the mainboard as a result


Additions:

+3 [[Giant Shark]]

  • As mentioned earlier in the primer, Giant Shark is basically [[Mariner's Curse]] copies 4-6. While it can hose us if we draw the wrong parts of our deck, the effect is strong enough that it can often lock the board state for turns at a time. I apologize to all the times I said you were bad, Giant Shark!

+1 [[Overflow]]

  • Turns out, ramp decks based off Landmass are a thing now! Finally, folks are catching on! To combat this, we increase our ability to ramp, too. Can't get locked out of mana if we lock them out first!

+1 [[Toolbox]]

  • Remember what I said about ramp decks? Yeah, we need to be aggressively ramping to compete with them. A third toolbox means we have six chances to deploy an Overflow on turn 3

+1 [[The Lady of the Lake]]

  • This card is the one I would categorize as "currently being tested." With the likelihood being very high that we will use Toolbox and Silver Bullet for early game advantage, it seems like a good idea to have a minion that can recur those cards for late game answers. Plus, she's a 3 power submerge unit in the worst case scenario.

+1 [[Makeshift Barricade]] (collection)

  • As mentioned in the primer, this is a meta answer to Zap. I also think it is strong as a way to stay off Death's Door, so it makes its way into the collection.

+1 [[Meat Hook]] (collection)

  • This card is absurd, especially with Giant Shark, but there are plenty of board states where Drown in the Deep has 0 minions in play. As a result, this lives in the collection, to be deployed when the board state is right for it.

+1 [[Swap]] (collection)

  • While we may not always want to draw Swap, its still absolutely busted. Its third copy lives here now.



2.3 - Minor Tweaks


More testing of cards and ideas from the gaggle of other Waveshapers has led to a few more tweaks, mostly to lock in the consistency of the deck's game plan. Below are the changes:


-2 [[Gloam Toads]]. +1 [[Guile Sirens]], +1 [[Anui Undine]]

  • With the lack of [[Pied Piper of Hameln]] decks and the continued prevalence of opposing [[Coy Nixies]], Guile Sirens and Anui Undine remain top tier picks in the current meta. Of the other units, Gloam Toads consistently underperformed, and opened the deck to submerge-based removal more often. As a result, I swapped them out in favor of the returning champions.

-1 [[The Flood]], +1 [[Swap]]

  • The naysayers were right! The Flood stinks! In the current meta, with water so prevalent, its actually a lot more rare that we need to flood the entire realm. While the pre-Gothic meta was begging for another [[Great Old One]] style effect, this meta just isn't the same. The Flood is gone in favor of Swap, an obscenely powerful card that is great at all points in the game.

-1 [[Abyssal Assault]] in the Collection, +1 [[Snowball]] in the Collection

  • While Abyssal Assault is an absolute powerhouse, the density of monsters has dropped too low in this list for it to be a consistent finisher. As a result, I've swapped it for a more consistent way to kill somebody on Death's Door.


2.2 - We're Not a Cult, I Swear


The Waveshaper community grows! After lots of discussion with players as passionate about Water as I am, the list has undergone a few minor tweaks, and a new section was added to the primer about updating the list to make it your own. Below is a summary of the card changes:


-1 [[Guile Sirens]], -1 [[Putrid Presence]], +1 [[Lilith]], +1 [[The Green Knight]]

  • These uniques are too strong to overlook, and have made their way into the list accordingly. While not directly synergistic with the list, they present insane card advantage the moment they hit the table, and push us even further ahead if they live for even a turn.

-1 collection copy of [[Extinguish]], +1 collection copy of [[Grievous Insult]]

  • While I was worried about Drought, the rise of mono-Water has led to a more dangerous tech piece: [[Old Salt Anchorman]]. As a result, I've included an extra way to turn off a unit that can't be drowned, whether they be unable to move or simply have submerge.


These cards are on my radar to test more, but may not make the cut:


  1. [[Wave of Eviction]] - an incredibly powerful forced movement tool, its only drawback is the inability to properly deal with the things it forcibly moves. While it can combo with other cards in our arsenal, the fact it doesn't replace itself and requires an extra card to do more than stop a few attacks means it feels awful to draw in any game where we're ahead or at board state parity.
  2. The 3rd Copy of [[Swap]] - many decks inspired by this one are on 3 copies of Swap, and rightly so; the card is busted. However, I've rarely had games where I want to draw more than one Swap, but would've loved to draw more board wipes. As a result, I've elected to keep it out in favor of...
  3. [[The Flood]] - the card currently keeping this list on 2 Swaps, [[The Flood]] is in an interesting spot. If the meta remains more heavily weighted towards non-water decks, then a second way to flood the entire realm is required. However, as more of the meta shifts to water, it becomes harder to justify this card.
  4. The 2nd Copy of [[Gloam Toads]] - while currently in the list, the fact that the Toads lack submerge means there's a chance one might get cut in favor of [[Guile Sirens]] number 3. However, their high power makes them more difficult to remove than the Sirens for some decks, and makes them an ideal unit to position for an [[Abyssal Assault]] out of the collection.
  5. [[Sacred Stag]] - A potential way to protect key sites while also being a 4 power beater is good, but its lack of synergy with our core strategy makes this tough to justify. However, warding key sites might be very important if certain decks (like Archi) gain a significant portion in the meta, so it's on my list to test.


2.1 - Post-SorceryCon 2026


This list has now been rigorously tested through a gauntlet of 26 constructed games across SorceryCon. Between Side Events, the Main event, and testing games with other attendees, I learned a lot, and came away with one conclusion:


This list is nuts. In those 26 games, I lost only 8, putting me at a 69% win rate (nice). In the main event, I was 5-1 day 1, ending the day in 8th place. While I lost my two rounds on Day 2 to incredible players and mediocre draws, I made both games incredibly close, and take pride in knowing that I was one draw away from taking control of both of those games. Plus, both of those players made it to top 8.


Gone are the days where Waveshaper and mono-water control are the underdog, fighting against the hyper-aggressive meta that pre-Gothic Druid ushered in. With so many decks on slower game plans that rely on playing one or two big threats and protecting them, Mariner's Curse has never been better, and that means this deck has never been better.


However, I didn't quite get the list correct. I was 90% of the way there, but testing proved out a few key things.


  1. While Abyssal Assault is awesome, it's hard to keep the lower end of my monsters alive long enough to take advantage of it int he mainboard. As a result, I've cut back on the monster sub-theme and left the Abyssal Assault only in the collection as a finisher.
  2. Guile Sirens is incredible. Turns out, copies 4-6 of Coy Nixie helps this deck immensely. Plus, they break wards for free every turn, which won me several games.
  3. With how slow the meta is, more board wipes is a good thing. [[Wrath of the Sea]] returns to the list as a result.
  4. [[Font of Life]] is still busted, especially with so much water in the meta. I thought I could cut down to just one in the collection, but there isn't a single game I played where drawing extra copies of Font would have been bad.


This is likely where the list will remain over the coming months, barring any significant shake-ups to the meta or any changes proven out by additional practice games.


2.0 - Post-Gothic Build and Testing Plans


You're reading 2.0 right now! Gothic is a massive shake-up to both this deck and the meta at large. The plethora of new forced movement effects, the powerful new units and monster synergies, and the backup copy of Mariner's Curse that is Thin Ice has fundamentally changed the power-level of this deck in ways I did not expect. Additionally, the meta has slowed down significantly, with less of an emphasis of value-based aggro and more of an emphasis on midrange. These changes are both great news for this deck, allowing us to trim previously necessary cards like [[Amulet of Niniane]] and [[Blasted Oak]] in favor of more cards that synergize with our core strategy.


In terms of testing, I'm still evaluating the exact number of each spell in the deck. Namely, I have my eyes on [[Font of Life]], [[Wave of Eviction]] and [[Overflow]]. I'm very high on Font of Life and Overflow, but I'm unsure how necessary they are in the slower meta. Jumping ahead on curve seems very powerful, hence why I'm on the full playset of Overflow, and gaining back lots of life can really move the game in our favor, but they may not be necessary depending on how well positioned we are in the meta. Similarly, [[Wave of Eviction]] is one of the strongest forced movement effects I've ever seen, but with so many excellent forced movement effects in our minion selection, I'm not sure its necessary.


Likely, I will be altering the count of spells and specific effects as I work to identify exactly which of the pillars of the deck need to be increased or decreased in the current landscape.

deckinfo.name: All Gas No Brakes
deckinfo.primer:
Get the opponent to deaths door as fast as possible.


Get to 4 sites and start double drawing.


Once opponent is at deaths door double drawing spells with sorcerer will likely find you the death blow very quickly.


Look to put as much pressure on as possible by constantly casting cheap minions.


Cheap minions are often weak, but with sorcerer you dont really mind if you lose a few minions along the way, especially when 10 of them have lethal.


The idea is if your playing two minions a turn and they are playing one a turn or even miss a turn of playing a minion


You just attack attack attack and they wont be able to defend everything.


Blade of thorns hits like a truck, and makes it pretty hard to kill your minions when They are 5 and 6 power.


The movement sites are so helpful


Sacred scarabs are awesome, being able to threaten a 4 damage dive bomb to their avatar or to one of their minions is really nice


This deck wants to go first to grab the momentum and try to never let go.


But with sorcerer if you fail to grab the early momentum it is pretty easy to shift into playing a little bit more patient game of work to run them down on cards and double draw to make up for it in the later game


you can really find some sneaky/ clever movement lines with the wuthering heights and river rapids paired with river of blood and river of flame. add a war horse to that mix and oh boy.

Also props to @Death's Door Podcast and @zachattack who developed their own versions of Earth/Fire Sorcerer aggro at the same time that I was working on Fury Road. It’s been awesome chatting with all three of you about decklists and card considerations over the past couple of months!


First month playtesting results: 103 Wins - 20 losses - 1 draw

I’ve stopped recording playtesting matches at this point but the overall winrate that I’ve had is about the same at close to 85%

16-2 against Avatar of Earth

16-5 against Deathspeaker

1-0 against Enchantress

23-3-1 against Pathfinder

10-2 against Avatar of Air

6-1 against Seer

4-1 against Geomancer (another game where Crown of the Victor did absolutely nothing.)

7-1 against Battlemage (2 of these games I drew Crown and it never had a use. Crown has been cut after brief testing.)

7-2 against Elementalist

1-0 against Flamecaller

7-2 against Sorcerer

5-1 against Sparkmage



Greetings, Sorcerers!

Aggro in Sorcery: Contested Realm is a bit different from other games that I've played like Magic: The Gathering and Flesh and Blood. The grid system slows combat down in the early game a LOT and that may be discouraging for lovers of Aggro strategies who are familiar with the concept as it plays in other games. Fear not! Aggro is still viable in Sorcery. You just have to approach it with the understanding that the pace of the game is set by how you and your opponent utilize the grid and deploy your minions and spells.

The goal of this particular build is to summon efficient minions whose overall power is greater than their mana cost in order to overwhelm opponents who are looking to play a longer, slower game. This deck is also great at putting down aggressive starts from the opponent and then grinding them into the dirt through pure attrition. One of the classic weaknesses of Aggro strategies is their tendency to fold once they run out of gas. It's nice to be able to start fast and strong but if you lose 3 minions to an Earthquake on your opponent's 4th or 5th turn, you may find yourself in a position where your smaller, more efficient minions are now outclassed by your opponent's larger threats. This is where the [[Sorcerer]] Avatar really shines. Being able to function well at 4-6 total mana means that at the time in the game where you would typically be running out of spells to cast, you can simply start drawing two cards from the Spellbook each turn. Most other Avatars won't be able to keep up with an you drawing twice as many new cards.

Putting pressure on your opponent early in the game is important with this deck. The grid system will slow you down a bit compared to other card games where your creatures can just start swinging as soon as they are no longer summoning sick. Sites like [[Rift Valley]] and [[Imperial Road]] really help you start dealing damage early on as they both allow you to get a site placed adjacent to one of the opponent's sites as early as the first or second turn. Without either of these utility sites, the games can be a bit slower as you will have to place sites in a direct line towards the enemy. Many players will meet you in the middle though which is very helpful!


Core Strategy: Death by a Thousand Cuts

[[Vile Imp]], [[Colicky Dragonettes]], [[Quarrelsome Kobolds]], [[Firebolts]], [[Blaze]], and the Desert Sites are all great ways to pick off smaller minions. With clever placement/movement they can combine to take down much larger minions or deal the final blow once the opponent is at Death's Door (Deserts being excluded from this last option). Because of how the turn structure in Sorcery works, it can be easy to deal a point of damage to a minion with [[Arid Desert]] at the beginning of the turn and then forget about that damage later in the turn. After you've summoned a fresh minion, moved and/or attacked with your existing minions, and cast a spell or two, you might not be thinking about finishing off that opposing minion that was injured by the [[Arid Desert]]. By moving a [[Colicky Dragonettes]] or [[Quarrelsome Kobolds]] into position you can make sure that any damage dealt during the earlier parts of the turn don't go to waste! This may seem like a super basic concept but if the board begins to get cluttered in the mid/late game, it can be difficult to keep track of everything that is going on so stay sharp! Every point of damage counts when you're playing Aggro! The new rules update on Projectile origin does make this aspect of the deck less flexible but I think that it is still a solid strategy.


Wake up the Giantess!

When I first saw the card [[Slumbering Giantess]] I was immediately impressed by her incredible power to mana ratio and I started looking through the card database to find the best ways to wake her up. As it turns out, Fire has a ton of cards that are powerful in their own right but have the flexibility of being able to wake up our Sleeping Beauty so she can start pounding the opponent's face right away! [[Vile Imp]], [[Firebolts]], [[Heat Ray]] (currently out of the list), and all of the basic Desert Sites can immediately get the Giantess out of bed and into her brawling boots. [[Colicky Dragonettes]] and [[Quarrelsome Kobolds]] are some additional - albeit slower - ways of getting the job done.

One last method that involves a little more setup is [[Root Spider]]. If you play the Giantess above a burrowed Spider, her genesis trigger will never resolve. Just remember that you’ll need to move the Spider away before she can get to work.

The addition of [[Ring of Morrigan]] gives this deck another ping effect to help wake her up!


Side Synergy: The beefiest Kobolds you've ever seen.

[[Gigantism]] and [[Torshammar Trinket]] are great when you're trying to outclass a larger minion or take a bigger bite out of the opponent's life total but these cards get absurd when you use them to pump [[Quarrelsome Kobolds]]. Since the boost from these spells lasts for the whole turn, the Kobold's end of turn ability benefits from any additional power that they have. Your opponent might feel safe and cozy at 16 life but a Gigantic Kobolds will knock them to Death’s Door if you can attack and end up with them nearby the enemy Avatar at the end of the turn! With the inclusion of [[Wicked Witch]] you also have the ability to shut Kobolds off if you want by reducing it's power. This can be handy if they can't get into a good position during your turn.


The Jewels: Yes, they are very good!

I've seen and heard a lot of people mention that they think the Cores and Stone are overrated. Yes, they are at their worst when you draw them late in the game or when you need your Spellbook to deliver action rather than ramp. They are certainly not something that you need to play in every deck but they are good here. The sooner you can get to 5 mana, the sooner you can start activating the [[Sorcerer]] to double up on card drawing. If you can start drawing twice as many cards as your opponent earlier in the game, that will greatly increase your potential to win. In the late game the Cores and Stone can certainly be a liability as a bad top-deck when you need action but at that stage in the game, the [[Sorcerer]] allows you to simply draw another card so it is very unlikely that you won't be able to find anything relevant to play each turn. Any turn that you can draw two spells instead of one is fantastic and the Cores allow you to continue developing your mana without needing to draw from the Atlas. Taking a full turn to draw and play a Site is much worse than drawing a Core and another Spell.

  • I’ve tested additional off-element Cores and while having the fast mana early against some decks is very nice, there are match-ups where the fast mana isn't as necessary and the chance that they are dead draws in the mid/late game is much more of a liability. I think that the on-element Cores are good but I've decided that I don't want to go too heavy on the mana rocks. If you wanted to trim a single Core for more action in your Spellbook, I would recommend [[Ruby Core]] as the cut. The deck is already skewed towards Fire threshold than it needs to be to fit enough Deserts so the Earth threshold from [[Onyx Core]] is more valuable.
  • I'm trying out a list that cuts the Ruby Core. I've found that more and more people are picking up this deck or something similar and the Cores are not as effective in the mirror match. You do lose a bit of potential power against [[Pathfinder]] and [[Roots of Yggdrasil]] decks but for the current metagame, I think cutting the Ruby may be the right move.


Why are there only a few 4+ mana spells?

In a lot of deckbuilding scenarios you want to see a smooth curve with something to do on all of the relevant turns of the game with a higher concentration of spells in the middle of the curve (turn 3 usually). This deck has enough 2 drops to allow you to be able to cast two of them on the 4th turn of the game in a lot of situations. Additionally, something like a turn 4 [[Slumbering Giantess]] followed by a Desert to wake her up is an acceptable turn even if the mana from the fresh Desert goes to waste. [[Wills-o'-the-Wisp]] (currently out of the deck) can also help round out odd mana turns. With fewer 4+ mana spells, you are less likely to see them early in the game where they can keep you from playing on curve - something that is extremely important in aggressive strategies.


Few Colorless Utility Sites.

Since you really only need around 5-6 mana sources to fully function before you start drawing mostly from the Spellbook, it is important to have the Threshold that you need early on. Any colorless Sites that you draw mean that you are more likely to need to keep drawing from the Atlas to hit Threshold requirements when you would rather be drawing spells. [[Imperial Road]] is very important in this deck as it allows you to fight through defensive sites like [[Gnome Hollows]], and [[Free City]]. It is also incredibly powerful against any [[Pathfinder]] opponents.


The Long Game.

While this deck is Aggro in the sense that it can put a lot of early pressure on the board, it also has very solid late game grinding power fueled by the [[Sorcerer]]’s ability to outdraw many opponents. I’ve adjusted the deck a bit to function at 6 mana since Flame Wave is such an effective finisher.



Additional Individual Card Explanations:


For cards that have been tested and are currently out of the list, I’m keeping the explanation for why they were originally in the deck, why I’m not running them in the current iteration, and why they might come back in.


[[Town]] - Now that [[Archimago]] is the clear best avatar in the game, I've been less happy with [[Imperial Road]]. Giving your opponent extra mana when their eventual goal is to use [[Craterize]] or [[Arcane Barrage]] as a finisher is not a great idea. I've decided to go with Town instead as it is often able to give a 1-2 mana discount every turn and doesn't ramp the opponent. The spellbook has been adjusted to increase the amount of Exceptional minions as well.


[[Yellow Knight]] - With the increase in popularity of Midrange, the Lance helps you clear larger minions. The technical 2.5 power body also allows you to sneak this guy onto [[Gnome Hollows]].


[[Siege Giant]] - With how popular [[Perilous Bridge]] is right now, it's nice to have a way to fly units around. With Town, this is also just a great inclusion as a 4 power for 3 mana.


[[Cone of Flame]] (Currently out of the deck) - After a post-game talk with @Ilphikur I've been convinced to run Cone over [[Flame Wave]]. While [[Flame Wave]] does allow you to hit avatars in more locations than Cone, it is also more difficult to use when both players are at Death's Door. [[Cone of Flame]] never being a liability when you are at Door and being generally more useful in the mid-game makes me feel confident that this is a good adjustment.

After adding in a second copy of [[Blaze]], a [[Shatter Strike]], and [[Ring of Morrigan]], I'm feeling like this deck has enough finishers that are easier to cast and don't clog up your hand in the early game. As such, I've taken Cone of Flame out for the time being.


[[Ring of Morrigan]] - This card is very, very powerful. It wakes up your [[Slumbering Giantess]], it combos with the rest of the ping effects in the deck to help with efficient removal of nearby threats, and it gains you life you that you have a much easier time in the aggro matchups!


[[Morgana le Fay]] - The Atlas needed some tweaking to support more triple-Fire threshold but I think it is well worth it. Morgana is absolutely amazing and a much needed Spellcaster for this deck.


[[Redcap Powries]] - Charge is a very powerful ability and the power to mana rate on this card is quite nice. This deck wants to be attacking any chance it gets so the drawback on this card is worth the upside.


[[Shield Maidens]] - With [[Arcane Barrage]], [[Magic Missiles]], [[Druid]] + [[Drums of Doom]], and [[Ring of Morrigan]] all entering the expected meta shift, I wanted to have a nice silver bullet to mulligan towards in those matchups. This card is also fantastic if you expect to face a lot of Fire aggro.


[[Boudicca]] - This card is amazing if you ever get to untap with multiple minions on the board. Even if you only have a single good attack on an enemy Site, a 3-power minion that gives +3 to another minion for the turn is a good rate.


[[Brother Knight]] (Currently out of the deck) - Very simple and very powerful. This deck loves dropping multiple minions in a single turn and that is tough the further up the curve you go. This card is a clean 2-for-1. There will be games where you draw both of them and that's going to be a bummer but I think it's still well worth including. I've cut [[Brother Knight]] for the time being. There are a lot of fire-based aggro decks in the meta right now and having both halves of this card trade for a single [[Vile Imp]] or [[Quarrelsome Kobolds]] has been feeling pretty rough. They've been replaced by [[Saracen Raiders]] for now.


[[Sir Morien]] (Currently out of the deck) - This card pairs very nicely with [[Boudicca]] and even without her, it's still a fantastic rate. Making 3 bodies and having the anti-projectile ability makes this card incredible against things like [[Grapple Shot]], [[Nelly Longarms]], and [[Pudge Butcher]]. Having some extra resistance to [[Firebolts]], [[Magic Missiles]], and [[Arcane Barrage]] is also really nice. Now that I'm running 3 copies of [[Town]], I had to cut Morien to make room for additional Exceptional minions.


[[Sir Priamus]] (Currently out of the deck) - Lethal and Lance are such good abilities together! This card is mainly a silver bullet option against [[Druid]] with [[Drums of Doom]] but the fact that it can always at least trade for 1 or 2 enemy minions regardless of their size is awesome.


[[Fields of Camlann]] - I'm not 100% sure if this is going to end up making the cut in the long run but it's worth testing out. The ability is very powerful but there are going to be times where you are the one with more minions on the board than the opponent. Luckily, most of your minions will be easy to replace because of their low cost and [[Sorcerer]]'s draw power.


[[Forge]] (currently out of the deck) - I'm not 100% sure that this is going to be better than an additional Desert site but Lance is a nice thing to have around when you're trying to get into combat and that is exactly what this deck is good at.


[[Poisoned Well]] (Currently out of the deck) - Holy cow, this card is amazing! This will typically be an easy 2-3 damage to the opponent which is wildly powerful for a Site. It gets a lot better if you have [[Rift Valley]] to really get into the middle of the opponent's home.

The damage from Deserts have been more relevant lately than the 1-2 average damage from Poisoned Well. As such, they're currently on the bench and replaced with additional Deserts.


[[Blaze]] - When I first started playing Sorcery, I underestimated just how important mobility on the grid would be. Since your opponent will likely use their turn to prepare for your next turn (specifically what you have on the board) being able to surprise them with extra movement can turn the game in your favor. At this point, most people have seen the power of cards like [[Blink]] and [[Grapple Shot]] but without Air, you need to dig a little deeper if you want to get access to more mobility. [[Mad Dash]] drawing you a replacement spell is really nice in a deck like this that is looking to start casting two spells per turn in the mid to late game but the extra movement and damage output from [[Blaze]] makes all the difference in a lot of situations. I originally started with a single copy of [[Blaze]] mostly as a late-game finisher for an opponent already on Death's Door. Repositioning Sorcerer to line up [[Firebolts]] or simply moving [[Quarrelsome Kobolds]] or [[Colicky Dragonetttes]] within range of the enemy was great! After playing with [[Wicked Witch]] for a while now, I'm realizing how good the combo is and I'm up to the full 3 copies of [[Blaze]] and I can't imagine going back down to a lesser number. This card has over-performed every time I see it and is responsible for tons of wins!

*The current list is running 0 copies of [[Wicked Witch]] so I've shaved down to a single [[Blaze]].


[[Infiltrate]] (Currently out of the deck) - I am back to zero copies in the maindeck. Archimago has virtually nothing you'll want to steal and the other aggro decks are so low to the ground that 4 mana is just too much for what you're likely to be able to target. Don’t forget that you can [[Infiltrate]] a spellcaster to finish the game with [[Firebolts]]!



[[Earthquake]] - You don’t usually want to draw this card early but there is no denying its power. When I initially built this deck, I didn’t consider how valuable rearranging the sites could be. As an aggressive deck, access to your opponent’s sites is very important and being able to Quake a hiding avatar into the line of sight for a [[Firebolts]] finish is great. Pulling their avatar towards one of your sites can also set you up to kill with [[Colicky Dragonettes]], [[Vile Imp]], [[Quarrelsome Kobolds]], or just a simple attack. Even if you have to kill some of your own minions with [[Earthquake]], you can easily replace those cards since at that point in the game, you’re just drawing two spells per turn. I may end up wanting two copies main but I feel like there are some decks where the effect is not needed or decks that use a lot of Water sites so I’m splitting the difference.


[[Smokestacks of Gnaak]] - There are several problematic sites that your opponen t can play against you. [[Gnome Hollows]], [[Great Wall]], [[Mountain Pass]], and especiallly [[Free City]] are all serious issues that impede your game plan. If you do go long against a [[Roots of Yggdrasil]] deck, Smokestacks is probably the best card you can have.


[[Pillar of Zeiros]] - This card is really nice against Deathspeaker in particular but it can also be incredibly powerful in any damage race situation you may find yourself in. Don't forget that you should play this card for little or no value if you suspect that your opponent is also holding a Pillar of their own. Denying them the life is often more important than waiting to gain a bunch of life yourself.


[[Flame Wave]] (Currently out of the deck) - Sometimes I’ve found the lack of Spellcasters in the deck can lead to games that are difficult to close out if the opponent has positioned their avatar out of projectile and Vile Imp range. While you don’t necessarily want to get up to 6 mana right away with this deck, you do want to get to 5. Because of this it means that you only ever need to simply draw and play your 6th site if you have [[Flame Wave]]. This card is one of the few auto-mulligan cards if it’s in your opener but the ability to kill an opponent at Death’s Door without needing to worry about board position is super valuable. So far, this card has felt great! With the addition of [[Wicked Witch]] there are more spellcasters in the list but [[Flame Wave]] is still excellent.


[[Jihad]] - This card offers a nice way to finish an opponent at Death's Door when you pair it with something like [[Vile Imp]], [[Colicky Dragonettes]], or [[Quarrelsome Kobolds]]. I'm testing a list with more Fire Minions right now and Jihad has come back into the deck after a long time sitting on the sidelines.


[[Torshammar Trinket]] - While watching coverage of the West Virginia Courtesan Cup Qualifier I noticed that Scott/@bubba was running Fire/Earth Sorcerer Aggro had two Trinkets in their list and I really liked the look of that card, especially in the mirror match. It allows all of your minions to kill their enemy dopplegangers without actually having to trade! I played with a single copy of [[Overpower]] for a while since it worked well with the Kobolds and allowed your [[Root Spider]]s to eat the opponent's Spiders. Trinket does both of these things and just keeps coming back to your hand for infinite value. While you can't tutor for it with [[Common Sense]] like you can with [[Overpower]] I still think that it's a great inclusion in the deck.


[[Aramos Mercenaries]] (Currently out of the deck) - This card has felt fantastic in testing so far and I think that it may be here to stay. There is a lot more control in the current meta (as of April 2024) and more and more decks are able to deal with a single threat per turn for the first 2-5 turns of the game after which, they can bring sweepers like Earthquake, Major Explosion, and Death Dealer online. Getting underneath control decks and taking huge bites out of their life total before they can stabilize has become more difficult when you're plan is to simply curve out with a 2-drop on turn 2, a 3-drop on turn 3, etc. Some control lists like @Zalem's Enchantress runs over 20 removal spells starting at 2 mana. One way to beat this strategy is to drop multiple minions per turn early in the game and then continue playing at least one minion per turn after that. If you can land a Bosk Troll and a Mercenaries on turn 2, or a Dragonettes and Mercenaries on turn 3, you'll be in a good position to keep the damage flowing.

Discarding a random card can feel scary and there are definitely some times where you will want to wait to discard but in most cases, just go for it. The extra minion on the board will very helpful most of the time. Another cut for Exceptionals while I test [[Town]].


[[Bedrock]] (Currently out of the deck) - The cat is out of the bag with [[Roots of Yggdrasil]] and as such, the 3 interchangeable tech slots in the Atlas have all been dedicated to [[Bedrock]] at this point. If you're against [[Seer]], [[Elementalist]], or otherwise know that your opponent is on a Roots plan, you'll want to mulligan aggressively towards [[Bedrock]]. [[Smokestacks of Gnaak]] is also good in these matchups (particularly against Elementalist), but most Roots decks can move their sites around using [[Earthquake]] or [[Atlas Wanderers]] so depending on your placement of Smokestacks, it may or may not be very effective in the long run. If and when Roots becomes less popular (or if you simply don't expect to play against Roots very often) you can cut 2 copies of [[Bedrock]] and use some combination of [[Gnome Hollows]] and [[Holy Ground]]. *With the increase to a 30-card Atlas, Roots has fallen off a bit and as such, [[Bedrock]] is out of the list for now.


[[Courtesan Thaïs]] - This is another piece of anti-Roots tech and is particularly good against Roots players who are using [[Scorched Earth]]. Thaïs is also fantastic against [[Deathspeaker]] decks running [[Nimbus Jinn]]. You typically don't want to see this card when playing against other aggro decks but it can still be very useful as a finisher once your opponent is at Death's Door. Now that [[Archimago]] is the clear best avatar, Courtesan is back in.


[[Sand Worm]] (Currently out of the deck) - We are finally at the end of the line in terms of the Burrowing arms race. It started out with [[Cave Trolls]] being added as part of the [[Common Sense]] package to deal with [[Root Spider]]s and now that enough people are running the Trolls, it's time for something a little larger. Landbound can definitely be a massive disadvantage against water but overall, [[Sand Worm]] is good enough in most situations to warrant a singleton slot. With the release of Arthurian Legends, I expect a lot more Water sites in the meta and this makes [[Sand Worm]] a rather dubious choice. We'll see how the meta shakes out but for now, I'm cutting it and going back to running [[Cave Trolls]] to deal with opposing [[Roots Spiders]].


[[Wicked Witch]] (Currently out of the deck) - @zachary showed me the power of this card paired with all of the small damage abilities in this deck. It also helps to fix the issue of not having many spellcasters to close the game with Firebolts which is really nice. I think I want to try to find room for one additional Earth site to help support it. As it stands, if you mulligan towards Earth, you may find yourself unable to cast Dragonettes and with the Witch being a 4-drop you have a bit more time to dig for threshold so it's possible that 8 Earth is enough but I'm going to see how it feels. Sequencing becomes much more important with the Witches in your deck. Make sure to make any aggressive plays first before playing her nearby or you’ll lose out on damage. Because her ability affects both players’ minions, maneuvering on the board can become difficult if you’re trying to push damage after playing her. I do really like the idea of her weakening effect paired with a [[Warp Spasm]] to just gobble up every 2 or less power minion on the board as long as they aren’t too spread out!

*I'm currently trying out a more aggressive list without Witches. This is mainly due to the decrease in people playing as much aggro in the current meta.


[[Outback Strider]] (Currently out of the deck) - With the new rules update about defending and movement, I wanted to give this card a try. I've also been considering [[Warp Spasm]] as a nice way to potentially clear a lot of enemy minions and then hit the opponent for a good chunk of their life total afterwards. Strider and Spasm seem like they will play together pretty nicely! I like having the [[Petrosian Cavalry]] as a target for [[Common Sense]] but it's tempting to cut it for a second Strider.


[[Swiven Scout]] (Currently out of the deck) - With the rise in popularity of Fire/Earth Aggro, players have been working on various ways to combat the deck. Two cards that have seen a sharp increase in play are [[Gnome Hollows]] and [[Free City]]. With these sites being more popular, [[Bosk Troll]] on turn 2 has been less effective. This deck still wants 2-mana minions and Scout feels like a pretty good swap. The fact that Scout is more vulnerable in the mirror match is an issue but it is somewhat mitigated by her +1 movement. You can place her out of reach of Kobolds and Imps but still be able to move up into striking range on your following turn.

Where this card really shines is in control or midrange matchups. Seeing your opponents hand is insanely powerful in most situations. In Sorcery you have almost no way to interact with your opponent on their turn outside of defending with your units. Because of this, the game is all about planning in advance based on what’s on the board and what your opponents are likely able to play on their next turns. With your opponent’s hand revealed, you’ll only be caught off-guard by top-decked spell which gives you a massive advantage. This ability has become increasingly powerful with the uptick in Roots decks that are solidifying their position in the meta.

The additional movement allows her to cruise through [[Free City]] to strike another site or get even more value out of [[Blaze]]!


[[Panorama Manticore]] (Currently out of the deck) - This is the most expensive card in the deck but I think it is worth it. The ability for this card to be able to attack and then untap to defend is wildly powerful. I also feel like it's important to have at least some Airborne options in a deck that is primarily looking to win the game through attacking with minions. This is a card that you will often mulligan from your opening hand to ensure that you have a smoother curve for the early game. You really don't want to draw this until turn 4-5 or later in most games. One thing that I have noticed about running this card is that it is the only card in the deck that you really feel bad about having hit by something like [[Bury]]. Most of the time you are able to drop two minions/spells per turn but with Manticore costing your entire turn to play, it allows the opponent an opportunity to effectively trade 1-for-1 which is something that you don’t want. While this card feels very powerful and like a must-answer threat, it’s entirely possible that they should just be swapped out for additional smaller minions.


[[Wills-o'-the-Wisp]] (Currently out of the deck) - This card is a fantastic way to start getting damage in early as well as being a seriously annoying card in the late game that can keep you safe from huge attacks from Earth or Battlemage decks. It also works well at chasing down opponents who are hiding on a Cloud City! I’m not running [[Jihad]] at the moment which makes smaller Fire minions slightly less appealing. I also haven’t found myself needing it as a chump blocker as much as I had imagined so I’ve cut it for now. If I start feeling a lot of pressure from large minions, and/or if [[Jihad]] ends up back in the deck, I’ll add Wisps again...

The Persecutor has really good mobility and removal. This is a simple deck, but can actually be pretty cerebral and fun to play.
